headline: A 'Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan' test: Risks of reforms without consultation
content: You can find a more diplomatic or politically convenient description for it, but the Modi government’s latest move on the Agniveer scheme, brought in with such aplomb, is a rollback. More so, a poll-eve capitulation. Seventy-five per cent of the first lot of Agniveers would have finished their tour of duty, or walked the Agnipath (path of fire), as the scheme was named, and returned to their hometowns and villages by December. It’s just that many would have gone back to Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand and Punjab, even Manipur, all going to the polls this coming February. All are traditionally major catchment areas for armed forces recruitment. For the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the first two are much too vital to risk. The prospect of these demobilised soldiers returning and joining opposition rallies, even enrolling in something like the Cockroach Janta Party, was scary for the BJP which, until the other day, was riding an all-conquering confidence. Now, it was seen as a risk not worth taking. On top of these, in November or thereabouts next year, Himachal Pradesh and Gujarat will have their state elections. Gujarat, the BJP can still be calm about. But Himachal, a stronghold it lost to the Congress last time, is a traditional recruiting area with a large ex-servicemen’s constituency. The party has now become far too risk-averse to put to the electoral test what was once its favourite reform. Reform it was, though. And we’ll talk about how, and then why it collapsed at its first test. There are three things governments are remembered for. Then there’s a fourth category: The good ideas a government implements and then withdraws under pressure or in panic. The good and the bad ideas are the first two. The third is the good ideas they propose but lack the nerve or skills to implement. We can list many of the United Progressive Alliance’s (UPA’s), for example: Aadhaar and India Stack based on it, direct benefit transfer (DBT) of welfare, even targeted delivery of subsidised cooking gas only to the poor and deserving. So were its many grand and audacious infrastructure projects of national importance. All got caught either in its indecision loop, internal party-versus-government contradictions, or ideological opposition. Most were subsequently consummated by the Modi government. Think the rail link to Srinagar, Mumbai Metro, Trans Harbour Link, the new Expressways, completion of the dedicated freight corridors (DFCs) and even the annihilation of armed Maoism. All of these were UPA projects abandoned midway. The Modi government did a brilliant job with these. It just tripped up on some of its own ideas. In journalism, we follow the three-example rule, meaning that these make a straight line. Or your argument. For Modi government’s rollbacks, count the farm laws, brought in with such self-assurance in 2020 and rolled back in their entirety in 2021 in the face of opposition from farmers. The second is now the Agniveer scheme. For the third, my preference would be the caste Census. The Modi government was opposed to it forever, then suddenly included it in the delayed 2021 Census being carried out now. This was under Rahul Gandhi’s pressure. If you don’t think that’s strong enough to make the third example —although I think it does, given the implications — I can give you another. The Prime Minister repeatedly derided the freebie culture, or what he contemptuously dismissed as “revdi” culture. Speaking at the inauguration of the Bundelkhand Expressway at Jalaun in UP in July 2022, he said, “This revdi culture is very dangerous for the development of the country. Those with revdi culture will never build new expressways, new airports or defence corridors for you.” And then, around the time of the Chhattisgarh elections in the winter of 2023, he announced that the Covid-era free food grain scheme would continue. In the same set of elections, the BJP brought in the Ladli Behna Yojana for cash transfers to women. Then, probably stung by the loss of majority in 2024, the party unleashed an almighty revdi “revolution”, with payouts reaching up to  ₹10,000 as a one-time transfer in Bihar and a promise of  ₹2 lakh if the woman started an enterprise. This was so expensive that even a rich state like Maharashtra is struggling to pay out, looking for excuses to reduce the number of beneficiaries. Women are already protesting, saying they’ve been denied their “Ladki Bahin” payouts. If you prefer, you can list this as the third example. However you look at it, this government has lost much of its appetite for risk, even with reforms where it had shown great conviction and commitment. These four examples are enough to show that the Modi government will also be remembered for the really good ideas it brought in, Agnipath included, and rolled back. This column, for the record, had supported each of these ideas. Between the farm laws and Agnipath, you could say the Modi government failed the test of both elements of the “ Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan” sentiment. It erred in taking its most significant and loyal constituencies for granted: Hindi heartland farmers and soldiers. The most disappointing thing is how it failed to reach out to them and build acceptance for such radical changes. People are by and large suspicious of major policy shifts with such significant implications for their lives, particularly when introduced through a shock-and-awe approach. That, however, has been this government’s style. Think sudden demonetisation or the Covid lockdown. Decisions affecting farmers and soldiers were taken in much the same way. Unlike the first two, which came with an end date, these policy changes were meant to survive in perpetuity. That explains the pushback from the base, and the Modi government’s rollback. Governance remains a painstaking, laborious, even boring business because it requires background work, scenario-mapping, war-gaming, or what the armed forces would call staff work. That is what the civil services and bureaucracies are there for. The absence of this precise element has bedevilled these plans — surprising, given how heavily the Modi government depends on civil servants. Were they asked to do their homework, or handed the decision first? There may be a concern that decisions could get caught in an analysis-paralysis loop. But you can’t always be like a commando who jumps out of a plane without checking the parachute. That isn’t fearless. It’s reckless. When Agnipath was implemented, it was well known that the first lot would leave on the eve of these state elections. An extensive rehabilitation programme, beginning midway through their four years, could have cushioned the blow. Now, the baby is gone, and with it the bathwater. The same lack of homework preceded the implementation of One Rank, One Pension (OROP). It was an election promise, all parties agreed with it, and no Indian would begrudge soldiers this benefit. But if the additional costs had been calculated and a necessary top-up provided to the defence budget, the story might have been different. The sudden increase in pensions because of OROP came from a defence budget that didn’t even keep pace with inflation over the years. This shrank the capital or acquisition budget. As concerns grew, Agnipath was rolled out in a hurry. Poor staff work created two kinds of soldiers, two sets of wages and even two sets of benefits for families in the event of a battle fatality. Most significant armies now have soldiers serving short tenures. But they don’t treat conscripted soldiers as a category separate from those on full-career service. Here, they were even addressed separately. Each unit then had an Agniveer sub-unit within it. This was unsustainable. The twin ideas of reducing the pension burden going ahead and making the armed forces much younger were both virtuous. Both have been lost to poor planning, hasty implementation and now withdrawal. This first batch will finish its sixth year on the eve of the 2029 general election. Rescuing this good idea will be a political miracle. It’s looking like a case of na khuda hi mila, na visaal-e-sanam (neither did I find God, nor my beloved). By special arrangement with ThePrint

headline: DA hike: Karnataka increases dearness allowance by 2.5%, and Arunachal Pradesh by 3% ahead of Diwali — Check details
content: DA hike news: The Karnataka and Arunachal Pradesh state governments have become the latest to increase dearness allowance for employees and pensioners after the Union Cabinet hiked DA by 3% for central government counterparts to 63% of basic pay.Karnataka hikes DA for employees, pensioners to 18%Karnataka on 5 November hiked DA and dearness relief (DR) for state government employees and pensioners drawing salaries under the 2024 Revised Pay Scales by 2.5%, from 15.75% to 18%, with effect from 1 July 2026, PTI reported.“Government employees are the backbone of our administration. Their dedication, professionalism and commitment are instrumental in translating our policies and programmes into meaningful outcomes for the people of Karnataka,” Deputy Chief Minister G Parameshwara said in a post on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter).“Equally invaluable is the contribution of our retired employees, who have devoted decades of their lives to public service and the progress of our state,” the statement added. It further said, “At a time when the cost of living continues to rise, it is our responsibility to safeguard the financial well-being and dignity of those who serve and have served our state. This enhancement is a recognition of their contribution and a measure of our commitment to supporting them and their families.” "The government remains committed to protecting the interests of employees and pensioners and recognising their contribution to public service, Parameshwara said. Arunachal Pradesh hikes DA, DR by 3% Arunachal Pradesh increased DA and DR for state government employees and pensioners by three percentage points, from 60% to 63%, effective from 1 July thsi year, as a “Diwali bonanza”, Chief Minister Pema Khandu announced in a social media post on Friday."I am pleased to announce that the government of Arunachal Pradesh has approved a 3% hike in DA for state government employees and DR for pensioners and family pensioners, increasing the rate from 60% to 63%, with effect from 1st July 2026," he said in a post on X.The enhanced DA and DR will also benefit All India Services (AIS) officers serving under the state government as well as central government employees on deputation to Arunachal Pradesh and will be paid along with the salary and pension for the month of November, he added.The CM said that arrears for the four-month period from July to October will be paid in cash and credited directly to the respective salary accounts of serving employees and the pension accounts of pensioners and family pensioners.DA hike announcements ahead of Diwali 2026DA is a percentage of employees' basic pay that aims to mitigate the impact of the rising cost of living and inflation. As per the 7th Central Pay Commission (CPC) recommendations, the Centre revises DA twice annually, using data from the All-India Consumer Price Index (AICPI).These announcements usually come in March and October, with rollouts in January and July. Effective from 1 July, the Centre's “Diwali gift” is the second DA increase this year, after it hiked the component by 2% in April from 58% to 60%, effective from 1 January for more than 1 crore beneficiaries.Notably, besides the Finance Ministry's announcement on 28 October, state governments also hiked DA for employees and pensioners ahead of Diwali. This includes a 5% hike by the Himachal Pradesh government, 3% DA hikes each by the Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan, Punjab and Gujarat governments, and 2% increases by the Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh and Kerala governments.(With inputs from Agencies)

headline: CM must stop claiming credit for BBMB verdict: Jai Ram | Hindustan Times
content: Former chief minister and leader of Opposition Jai Ram Thakur on Saturday welcomed the Supreme Court’s verdict on Himachal Pradesh’s electricity share in the BBMB but criticised chief minister (CM) Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu for trying to take political credit for it.He said the verdict was the result of nearly three decades of legal struggle, efforts by successive state governments, judicial intervention and support from the Central government.While addressing media in Shimla, Thakur said that the CM should refrain from portraying the judgment as his personal achievement. He emphasised that the verdict is a collective victory for the people of Himachal Pradesh and the culmination of a long struggle to secure the state’s legitimate rights.Tracing the history of the dispute, Jai Ram Thakur said that the issue of Himachal Pradesh’s rightful share arose following the reorganisation of Punjab in 1966. Former chief minister Shanta Kumar strongly advocated the concept of royalty on water resources, arguing that Himachal Pradesh deserved compensation for its natural resources.He recalled that the matter was taken to the Supreme Court in 1996 during the tenure of former CM Virbhadra Singh. Subsequently, on September 27, 2011, during the BJP government led by professor Prem Kumar Dhumal, the Supreme Court delivered a landmark judgment recognising Himachal Pradesh’s 7.19 % electricity share in the BBMB projects.“The most significant legal milestone was achieved in 2011 when professor Prem Kumar Dhumal was chief minister. The Sukhu government cannot erase this history merely because the final judgment has been delivered during its tenure,” Thakur said.He further explained that during his own tenure as CM, the Himachal Pradesh cabinet, on January 4, 2018, approved further negotiations regarding the return of differential energy. The state government continued pursuing the matter before the Supreme Court and with the concerned states.Thakur said that important developments took place during 2019 and 2020, including directions from the Supreme Court requiring the concerned parties to submit their positions. The intervention of the attorney general of India, representing the Union government, subsequently helped develop a practical cashless settlement mechanism.

headline: Himachal executes first inter-state Golden Mahseer fingerling shipment to West Bengal
content: Bilaspur (HP), Nov 7 (PTI) In a significant step towards exploring new horizons in fisheries and aquaculture, Himachal Pradesh's Department of Fisheries achieved a milestone by undertaking the first-ever interstate supply of Golden Mahseer (Tor putitora) fingerlings to West Bengal.This initiative marks an important step towards establishing Himachal Pradesh as a potential source of quality fish seed and promoting the commercial value of its indigenous fish species beyond the state, officials said on Saturday."The first-ever interstate supply of Golden Mahseer fingerlings to West Bengal represents a significant achievement for the Department and reflects the growing technical and institutional capacity of the state in fish seed production," said Director-cum-Warden of Fisheries, Himachal Pradesh, Om Kant Thakur.He said the state has immense potential in coldwater fisheries and indigenous fish species, and the department is committed to exploring new avenues for expanding the fisheries sector through scientific fish breeding, quality seed production, conservation and commercialisation.In the first phase, a consignment of 2,000 Golden Mahseer fingerlings has been supplied to West Bengal. The initial consignment has been deliberately kept limited to assess and monitor various transportation-related challenges, survival rates and acclimatisation requirements of the fingerlings under the climatic and environmental conditions of the destination state.Based on the successful transportation, survival and acclimatisation of this consignment, the department plans to supply the next lot of 10,000 Golden Mahseer fingerlings in the second phase.The fingerlings were raised at the National Mahseer Farm, Machiyal, District Mandi, an important facility for propagation and conservation of this valuable indigenous fish species. The consignment was sold to Subrata Mandal, a young fish entrepreneur from Dakshin Dinajpur, West Bengal.Golden Mahseer, scientifically known as Tor putitora, is one of the most valuable indigenous freshwater fish species found in the Himalayan river systems, including Himachal Pradesh.Belonging to the family Cyprinidae, this magnificent fish is popularly known as the 'Golden Mahseer' because of its attractive golden appearance.It is also the State Fish of Himachal Pradesh and holds considerable ecological, economic, recreational and cultural significance.The species is particularly popular among anglers because of its remarkable strength, fighting ability and sporting characteristics, making it one of the most sought-after game fishes in the Himalayan region. Besides its recreational importance, Golden Mahseer is also a valuable food fish and has considerable potential for commercial aquaculture and fish seed production.The species has been categorised as endangered on the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species, highlighting the importance of its conservation, scientific breeding and sustainable management.It plays an important role in maintaining the ecological balance of freshwater ecosystems and is considered a keystone/umbrella species for the health of riverine aquatic habitats. Its presence is also an indicator of the ecological quality of freshwater environments.In Himachal Pradesh, Golden Mahseer is an important component of reservoir fisheries, particularly in Pong and Gobind Sagar reservoirs, where it contributes to the biodiversity and fisheries resources of these water bodies.The species also supports the livelihoods of fishermen and contributes to nutritional security by providing a valuable source of protein. Its conservation and scientific propagation are therefore important not only from the biodiversity perspective, but also for the sustainable development of fisheries and the livelihood security of fishing communities.The department envisages that such initiatives will encourage greater investment in fish seed production, strengthen market linkages and enhance the income-generating potential of fisheries infrastructure. At the same time, conservation-oriented propagation of Golden Mahseer will contribute towards protecting this endangered indigenous species and maintaining the ecological health of Himalayan aquatic ecosystems, officials added.
